clips.title: Securing AI Agents: How to Prevent Hidden Prompt Injection Attacks
clips.why: A concrete story of an AI agent misled by text hidden in what it read, and how such agents work.
look: The agent did exactly what the hidden text said, not what its user wanted.
The agent reads untrusted content and can take actions: the same position Nova is in with a Jira comment.
Notice that the attack needs a way for the agent to act or send something out.
clips.after: Our answer does not depend on the model noticing the attack: the sandbox simply has nowhere to send our code except a short list of names.

clips.title: Proxy vs Reverse Proxy (Real-world Examples)
clips.why: What a forward proxy is and why organizations put one between their machines and the internet.
look: The forward proxy sits in front of the clients, not the servers.
One of its uses is blocking access to some sites.
The server sees the proxy, not the client.
clips.after: Our Squid is a forward proxy for the sandbox VMs, and blocking every site except the allow-list is its only job.

clips.title: Back to Basics: Providing Secure Connectivity with SaaS Applications with PrivateLink
clips.why: AWS explains PrivateLink: reaching one service in another network through a private endpoint, without joining the networks.
look: The provider side publishes a service behind a load balancer; the consumer side gets an endpoint in its own VPC.
Traffic stays on private addresses and never crosses the internet.
Why this is narrower than connecting whole networks.
clips.after: Our internal cluster publishes exactly three services this way, the broker, the gateway and the collector, and only to the ai-agents account.

practice.q: Nova runs npm ci in its VM. Put the trip of one package request in order.
items: npm reads HTTPS_PROXY from the environment
npm sends CONNECT nexus.rhinohealth.com:443 to the proxy
Squid checks the source subnet and the name against its rules, top to bottom
The allow rule matches, so Squid opens the tunnel and logs TCP_TUNNEL/200
npm talks TLS to Nexus through the tunnel; Squid never sees the content
practice.why: The proxy decides on the name in the CONNECT request before any data flows, which is why an allow-list works even though the traffic is encrypted.

practice.q: Which squid.conf rule order keeps the allow-list working?

options.text:
http_access deny all
http_access allow sandboxes whitelist
options.why: First match wins, so deny all matches every request and nothing is ever allowed. npm ci breaks.

options.text:
http_access allow sandboxes
http_access deny all
options.why: This allows sandboxes to reach any name. The list is never checked, and the upload works.

options.text:
http_access allow sandboxes whitelist
http_access deny all
options.why: A request must come from a sandbox and name a listed host to pass; everything else falls through to deny all.

practice.q: Finish the environment line so the harness reaches our own services over PrivateLink instead of through Squid.
practice.hint: Our private zone: broker., gateway. and otel. all live under it.
practice.why: Names in NO_PROXY skip the proxy. Our private DNS zone points them at the PrivateLink endpoint, so they never meet Squid's list.

practice.q: The proxy's access log shows 9 lines of TCP_DENIED/403 CONNECT pastebin.com:443 from one sandbox in three minutes. What does it most likely mean?

options.why: TCP_DENIED means Squid refused the request itself. The site was never contacted.

options.text: The run is probably following an instruction it found in its input, and a person should look.
options.why: Repeated refusals from one source are the signal for possible prompt injection. More than 5 in 5 minutes alerts #ai-agents-alerts and Security.

options.text: The allow-list is missing a name the run needs, so add pastebin.com.
options.why: A paste site is a classic place to drop stolen data. Never add a name because a run keeps asking for it.

practice.q: A sandbox without the proxy tries curl https://1.1.1.1. The VPC has no internet gateway and no NAT. Fill in what happens to the packet.
practice.after: out of the VPC, so the connection fails.
practice.hint: What a route table would need to point at an internet gateway.
practice.why: With no internet gateway and no NAT, no route leads out. That is the first wall, and it holds without any rule knowing what an attack looks like.
